senses: The black-necked stork, Ephippiorhynchus asiaticus.
ety: From a Tupian term such as Old Tupi îabyru, said to mean either "swollen neck" or "one that spits".
examples: He's a jabiru - the only Australian stork.

senses: Having the characteristics of a clique.
ety: From clique + -y.
examples: Do not form clubs on the playground that don't include everyone - they're cliquey and mean.
Cliquey is cooler. If you don't like it blame Kitch.

senses: To cause (someone) to go insane or become deranged.
To cause disorder in (something); to distort from its ideal state.
To cause to malfunction or become inoperative.
ety: From French déranger, from Old French desrengier (“throw into disorder”), from des- + rengier (“to put into line”), from reng (“line, row”), from a Germanic source. See rank (noun).
examples: Both these kinds of monopolies derange more or less the natural distribution of the stock of the society;

senses: A toastmaster at a feast in the Caucasus, especially in Georgia.
ety: Borrowed from Georgian თამადა (tamada), from (Proto-?)Circassian *tħamada (compare West Circassian тхьаматэ (tḥamatɛ, “foreman of a village; boss; master; chairman; (dated) husband”), East Circassian тхьэмадэ (tḥɛmadɛ, “foreman of a village; boss; master; chairman; (dialectal) bridegroom, wooer”)), possibly from Persian داماد (dâmâd, “bridegroom; son-in-law; father-in-law; sovereign's brother-in-law; lover, wooer”) with the ending reshaped under the influence of East Circassian адэ (adɛ, “father”). The suggestion that the word is derived from a blend of თავი (tavi, “head”) + მაგიდა (magida, “t
examples: We have the custom of a toastmaker – the tamada, we call him. For the sake of order, he proposes all the toasts. Will you support me as tamada?
This tamada had excellent rhetorical skills; he was fluent in both Russian and Kyrgyz and knew the languages of humor and honor.

senses: Having a reddish, coarse complexion, especially with a pudgy face.
Slovenly or unkempt, in the manner of a beggar or slattern.
Unrefined, countrified.
ety: From blows(e) + -y.
examples: Her hair so untidy, so blowsy!

The double-breasted blazer which is on every front row this season came with an elbow-length sleeve for spring, while jumpsuits, a signature of the label, came slinky and tailored or in a blowsier boiler suit silhouette.
The hot, blowsy country, remote from danger, had a lonely, forgotten feeling.

senses: Having freckles; covered with freckles.
ety: Inherited from Middle English frekled; equivalent to freckle + -ed.
examples: A smile grew across Jim's freckled face.

At any other time Jessamy would have laughed at the expressions that chased each other over his freckled face: crossness left over from his struggle with the baby; incredulity; distress; and finally delight.

senses: A poetic form mostly used for love poetry in Middle Eastern, South, and Central Asian poetry.
ety: Borrowed from Arabic غَزَل (ḡazal, “to display love to the loved one via speech, to exchange talk of love with the loved one”).
examples: Indeed, this is a realm where colors harmoniously recite magnificent ghazals to each other, where time stops, where the Devil never appears.
A poet could explain him to himself but he was a soldier and had no place to go for ghazals or odes.

senses: A small ornamental piece of lace or linen or paper used to protect a surface from scratches by hard objects such as vases or bowls; or to decorate a plate of food.
A similar circular piece of lace worn as a head-covering by some married Jewish women.
ety: From Doiley, the name of a 17th-century London draper. The surname is Anglo-Norman, from d'Œuilly, name of several places in Calvados, from Old French oeil (“eye”).
examples: Beg pardon, I'm soiling the doileys / With afternoon tea-cakes and scones.

senses: Containing starch.
Having the quality of fabric starch as applied to fabric; stiff, hard; starched.
Having a starched personality; stiffly formal.
ety: From starch + -y.
examples: Beds were made, the dinner-table set, and then we got into our very starchiest and most uncomfortable clothes for church.

senses: An Egyptian female singer or dancing-girl used for entertainment; sometimes a prostitute.
ety: Ultimately from Arabic عَالِمَة (ʕālima, “singer”), originally a feminine adjective meaning ‘learned, knowledgeable’, from عَلِمَ (ʕalima, “to know”).
examples: Nostalgia is almah, the Arab dancing girl. She tells me stories of the drowned, the deadest of this world's dead.

senses: Video games.
ety: Humorous alteration of video. Originates from the 1990s American sitcom King of the Hill. American regional usage far precedes this.
examples: There are a hundred angles to this issue and the criticism has been noted since video games first saw the light of day. However, I've never really examined the question: is "the vidya" bad for you?
Quinnae Moongazer, a pizza loving feminist sociologist and amateur slug herder, spends her time writing about feminism, transgender politics, and the vidya.
The site We Hunted The Mammoth scoured the full transcript released by 4chan, turning up gems from some anons like, "i couldnt care less about vidya, i just want to see zoe receive her comeuppance."

senses: A nocturnal dance held by Aboriginal Australians, for social, celebratory or warlike purposes.
A song or chant made for such a festivity.
Any noisy, late-night gathering or disturbance.
ety: Borrowed from Dharug garabara.
examples: A hundred yards or so away the throaty beat of a didgeridoo drifted down from some ancient corroboree, a splendid accompaniment to the music of the night
He reached home, and lived long enough to hear the natives wailing in a Death Corroboree over his late comrade.

senses: A small screw-tipped tool for boring holes.
A cocktail, usually made with gin and lime juice.
ety: From Middle English gimlet etc., from Old French guinbelet, guimbelet, guibelet, probably a diminutive of the Anglo-Norman wimble, a variation of guimble (“drill”), from the Middle Low German wiemel; continued in Modern French as gibelet. Cocktail either named after the tool, in reference to its penetrating effects, or British Navy surgeon Thomas Gimlette (1857–1943).
examples: The box was close on every side, with a little door for me to go in and out, and a few gimlet holes to let in air.
Yeah, a piece of advice — once you’re back in circulation, don’t keep topping off a lady’s vodka gimlet when she’s not looking.
By seven, dinner was under way, and a bottle of vodka gimlets and one of martinis were in the freezer, chilling.

senses: One who flexes something physically.
One who flaunts or shows off.
ety: From flex + -er.
examples: Muscle flexers and weight lifters have been given academic approval by a University of California scientist.

senses: The practice of following a vegetarian diet.
ety: Attested since circa 1847, when the British Vegetarian Society was founded. From vegetarian + -ism.
examples: Vegetarianism, he said, is an idea “that has three things going for it all at once—economics, health and compassion.”

Right now, my family’s special collision of vegetarianism and Judaism necessitates a good bit of chocolate. But when Passover ends, that doesn’t mean we should put the chocolate cake, or the chocolate milk, away.

senses: Of, being, containing, or pertaining to memes; pertaining to replication of concepts.
ety: From meme + -etic, by analogy with gene → genetic.
examples: But let’s not assume that all of the innuendo and debate is a product of the Russian info-war, or that the Kremlin is a grandmaster of the memetic chessboard.

Within different communities, groups, or dyads, the same memetic media could be deployed as a long-standing community in-joke, dadaist absurdity, or even as fighting words (or images, as the case may be).

Gamergate, “the Fappening” (or Celebgate), and the subsequent Comicsgate are examples of campaigns that deployed active memetic warfare in racialized and gendered ways to attack and drive away a constructed enemy.

senses: Filthiness and degradation, as from neglect or poverty
ety: From the Latin squālor.
examples: The heterogenous indigent multitude, everywhere wearing nearly the same aspect of squalor.
We’re living in squalor That’s the name of this house This house is called squalor by all There’s a door broken somewhere but I never can remember quite where.

senses: An ornamental cloth, often embellished with embroidery or jewelry, worn over the chest by women beneath their bodices or by men and women as the central part of an open shirt, blouse, or jacket.
A similar item of mail worn over and protecting the stomach.
A blow to the stomach.
ety: Inherited from Middle English stomakere, stomachere, perhaps after Anglo-Norman *estomachier. Equivalent to stomach + -er.
examples: Stomacher brooch of brilliants and fine oriental pearls.
Here, from the fading canvas, smiled Lady Elizabeth Devereux, in her gauze hood, pearl stomacher, and pink slashed sleeves.
From about 1850 onwards jewellery varied between these outsize sprays, stomachers and corsage montages and smaller, more delicate pieces which appeared almost understated by contrast.

senses: A form of government in which unlimited power is held by a single individual.
An instance of this government.
ety: From auto- + -cracy, from Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατία (autokratía, “A system of government by one person with absolute power.”), from αὐτός (autós, “single, self, same, alone”) + κράτος (krátos, “power”) + -ία (-ía, “feminine abstract nouns suffix”); see also Ancient Greek αὐτοκρατής (autokratḗs, “one who governs alone”).
examples: I want to be clear: This shift toward democracy and away from autocracy is no reason to break out the “mission accomplished” banner.
The will of the people of Ukraine to defend their democracy is a reminder that autocracies cannot ultimately overcome free people willing to defend their liberty.

senses: To express with the voice, to utter.
To produce noises or calls from the throat.
To sing without using words.
ety: From vocal + -ize.
examples: We could hear the monkeys vocalizing, though we could not see them.

senses: an attitude or expression of mocking irreverence and sarcasm.
ety: Noun sense “snide remark” as back-formation from snarky (1906), from obsolete snark (“to snore, snort”, verb) (1866), from Middle English *snarken (“to snore”), from Proto-West Germanic *snarkōn, equivalent to snore + -k. Compare Low German snarken, North Frisian snarke, Swedish snarka, German schnarchen, and English snort and snore. Of Germanic origin, but ultimately onomatopoeic.
examples: She liked his smile. There was neither snark nor megalomania in it, as characterized so many smiles these days.

senses: A rough carnelian bead, formerly used in Africa as currency when buying slaves for the slave trade.
ety: Rango is the earlier form, attested from 1644. From Malagasy rango (“long and thin”).
examples: There we purchased two sheep, one for two strings of arangoes, for the other I gave a note upon Mr. Walker for a bar of salt.

senses: An adjectival phrase or clause.
ety: From adjective + -al.
examples: Within this line of reasoning, then, Tagalog is classified as a language in which adjectivals are essentially neutral between a nouny and a verby interpretation.

senses: A traditional style of eatery having public seating and multiple vendors selling Chinese, Indian, and Malay food.
ety: Borrowed from Malay kopitiam, from Hokkien 咖啡店 (ko-pi-tiàm), in turn from Malay kopi (“coffee”).
examples: Bustling kopitiams sprouted around derelict whiskey bars like toadstools around rotting logs.

senses: An abalone or sea-ear, particularly Haliotis tuberculata, common in the Channel Islands.
ety: From Norman ormèr/ormer, variants of French ormier, contraction of oreille-de-mer, from Late Latin *auris maris (“ear of the sea”), from Latin auris (“ear”) + mare (“sea”).
examples: The food I like best of all foods is ormers; but you can't always get them.

senses: Furnished with buildings.
Built or constructed.
Morally or intellectually improved.
ety: From edify + -ed.
examples: The Pissaglio river alluvial fan is the area where about 90% of Bruzolo edified areas are located (Fig. 2) .
Summing up, the designed buildings' generic ontology intends to establish a generalist organization for edified structures, based on the CityGML standard.
Still in the colonial period, it began to be charged when it focused on the ownership of edified buildings.

senses: A pile in which junk is discarded.
A collection of discarded or rejected items or ideas.
ety: From scrap + heap.
examples: By Easter, "Princess Royal" Pacifics Nos. 46211/2 were in the scrap line at Crewe works and Nos. 46204/5/7/10 were gathered at Crewe South shed, no doubt to follow to the scrapheap.

senses: Master of ceremonies.
ety: Pronunciation spelling of MC (“master of ceremonies”).
examples: The emcee of the event, Ed Bejarana, called Borrenpohl a "little girl," at the town hall, saying: "This little girl does not want to leave. She spoke up and now does not want to suffer the consequences."

senses: To cause to move (suddenly), as by pushing or shoving; to give a (sudden) start to.
To divert to a less important place, position, or state.
To provide with a shunt.
To move a train from one track to another, or to move carriages, etc. from one train to another.
To have a minor collision, especially in a motor car.
ety: From Middle English schonten, schunten (“to jerk, swerve; to dodge, escape”), either: * possibly a back-formation from Middle English schonen (“to avoid, refuse, hate, fear”), from Old English sċunian, sċyniġan; see shun. Or * an alteration of Middle English *schunden, *schynden, from Old English sċyndan, sċendan (“to hasten, hurry”) (as in āsċyndan (“to remove, take away”), from Proto-West Germanic *skundijan, from Proto-Germanic *skundijaną (“to impel, hasten”). * from unrecorded Old English *sċunettan, a derivative of sċunian (“to shun, avoid”). As regards the noun sense, compare Middle Eng
examples: Porter, run over while shunting a luggage train, in consequence of his getting entangled in shunting-rope.

senses: The bride price among certain Bantu peoples of South Africa.
ety: From Xhosa lobola, Zulu lobola (“pay dowry”).
examples: The cattle of the second kaffir had been obtained from the first kaffir as lobola; all (three) have died from the disease.
My sister Baliwe, who was older than Mabel, had been engaged to be married, and lobola had already been paid.

senses: A type of footwear used in India, Mauritius, and Pakistan, similar to a sandal.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi चप्पल (cappal), itself borrowed from Telugu చెప్పులు (ceppulu).
examples: Chappals and shoes will fill up the garbage pit too quickly. I think it is impossible to burn old shoes and chappals. They melt and become very bad.

senses: A thicker form of spaghetti with a hole running through it.
ety: From Italian bucatini, diminutive of buco (“hole”).
examples: You could make this with spaghetti or linguine or other types of long skinny pasta, but bucatini are what's used in Rome.

senses: Like a spider.
Characterized by many spindly extensions.
Suggestive of cobwebs; spiderweb-like.
Infested with or containing many spiders.
Cramped or illegible; especially when spiky.
ety: From spider + -y.
examples: High up on the viaduct, and approached by a spidery staircase from the street, it looks down on Southwark Cathedral.
The spidery construction looked like it would fall apart in a stiff breeze.
This shelf is deeply cut into by rivers, so that the line has to cross a series of spidery lattice-girder bridges.

senses: Sexually aggressive or inappropriate in a way that causes fear or unease.
Suggestive of, or characterised by, rape.
ety: From rape + -y.
examples: This song is pretty rapey if you think about the lyrics.
If this all sounds a bit “rapey,” that's only because there were different standards of morality back in the days of Greek mythology.
Because this is a man, let's say you're on a date and some guy comes out of the alley with a knife and a rapey kind of vibe.

senses: mildly hungry
irritable; crotchety
ety: From peck (verb) + -ish. From late 18th century.
examples: After that run, I'm feeling a bit peckish.

senses: A steep descent or declivity; steep face or edge of a ridge; ground about a fortified place, cut away nearly vertically to prevent hostile approach.
ety: Borrowed from French escarpement. By surface analysis, escarp + -ment.
examples: The railway winds down the face of the escarpment on a steady grade of 1.05 per cent, which is considerably better than the old route, up which trains took 2 hr. to struggle 15 miles, with two stops.

senses: The act of passing back; passage back; return; retrogression.
The power or liberty of passing back.
ety: (verb) From Latin regressus, past participle of regredior (“to go back”), from re- (“back”) + gradior (“to go”). Doublet of regressus.
examples: The key-hole was still their port of egress and regress, and it resembled the aperture of a bee-hive, on a sunny day in June.
Its bearing on the progress or regress of man is not an inconsiderable question.
Thou shalt have egresse and regresse.

senses: A child of noble birth.
The cognomen given to the oldest son prior to his taking his father's title.
A vampire who was turned by another vampire (the childe's sire) in a particular way.
ety: From Old English ċild.
examples: Childe Rowland to the dark tower came. His word was still "Fie, foh, and fum, I smell the blood of a British man."
She had waded in blood and reveled in death, she had torn her enemies asunder with shadow and given their childer to the flame.
Alexander, the ancient vampire who has ruled Paris for many centuries, has been deposed by his own childe, Sir Geoffrey.

senses: Contrary to something; discordant.
Abhorring; detesting; having or showing abhorrence; loathing.
Detestable or repugnant.
ety: Borrowed from Latin abhorrēns, abhorrēntis, present active participle of abhorreō (“abhor”). Equivalent to abhor + -ent.
examples: This legal, and, as it should seem, injudicious profanation, so abhorrent to out stricter principles, was received with a very faint murmur, ...
If Pride, abhorrent as it is, and if Ambition, ...
That, I protest, is a doctrine psychologically impossible and ethically abhorrent.

senses: Mist, fog, vapour.
ety: Borrowed from French brume, from Latin brūma (“winter solstice; winter; winter cold”). Brūma is derived from brevima, brevissima (“shortest”), the superlative of brevis (“brief; short”) (the winter solstice being the shortest day of the year), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *mréǵʰus (“brief, short”).
examples: For, shou'd you come before the Brume's abated / Th' Opime you'd linquish for the Macerated.
All around their bubble of stupidity I could feel the brume of the dragon.
